segments.translit:
śrīmatsatguruvaktrapaṅkajarasāsvādasphuraddhīdayo
natvā śrīkuliśeśamaddvayadhiyaṃ śraddhāprasannānanaḥ|
śrīlūyīcaraṇādisiddharacite'pyāścaryyacaryyācaye
sadvartmāvagamāya nirmmalagirāṃ ṭīkāṃ vidhāsye sphuṭam||
segments.translation: My wisdom and compassion shining from tasting the nectar of the lotus mouth of the glorious true [guru]{guru}, my face serene with faith, I bow to the glorious Lord of the [vajra]{vajra}, whose understanding is nondual, and so that the true path may be understood I will compose a clear commentary, in stainless words, on the collection of wondrous songs of [conduct]{carya} composed by the [siddhas]{siddha}, beginning with the venerable [Lūyī]{p-luyi}.
segments.note: Munidatta opens with his own verse of homage. Having tasted the nectar of the true [guru]{guru}'s lotus mouth and bowed to the Lord of the [vajra]{vajra}, he promises a clear commentary on the wondrous songs of [conduct]{carya} composed by the [siddhas]{siddha}, [Lūyī]{p-luyi} first among them, so that the true path may be understood.

flags.note: -dhīdayo is taken as dhī + dayā, 'wisdom and compassion'. A reading dhī + udaya, 'whose understanding has risen shining', would normally give -dhyudaya, so I set it aside.
śrīkuliśeśam advayadhiyam: advayadhiyam may qualify the Lord ('whose understanding is nondual', chosen) or stand in apposition ('the Lord of the vajra, nondual understanding itself').

nirmmalagirāṃ (genitive plural) could describe the commentary ('in stainless words', chosen) or the siddhas ('of stainless speech'). caryā in āścaryyacaryyācaye stands for the caryā songs themselves, hence 'songs of conduct'. The particle 'pi after racite looks metrical and is not translated.

segments.translit:
rāgapaṭamañjarī—kāātaruvaretyādi| śrīmadgurucaraṇāravindamakarandavindusandohaśāntasantarpitānandastimitahṛ[da]yaḥ satyadvayamahāmohabhramajaladhimadhyanimagnā'śaraṇadīnajanasamuddharaṇakāmo hi siddhācāryya [2] śrīlūipādaḥ praṇidhipreritāvatāraṇārthaṃ kāataruvyājena suddhadharmmatāpīṭhikāṃ prākṛ[ta]bhāsayā racayitumāha kāyetyādi| rūpādayaḥ pañcaskandhāḥ| ṣaḍindriyāṇi dhātavo viṣayāśca grāhyagrāhakagrahaṇopalakṣitapallavatvāt kāyataruvaratvena gṛhītaḥ| nanvacetanatvāt kathaṃ kāyastaruvaraḥ| naiṣa doṣaḥ|
tathaiva bahiśāstrakārairapyutprekṣālaṅkāraparaiḥ kiñcid bhedādhiṣṭhānaṃ hi sādṛśyamudīritaṃ| kimutāsya prakṛtyābhāṣadoṣavaśāt cāñcalyatayā prākṛtasattvenācyutirūpo hi rāhuḥ| sa eva kālaḥ| kṛṣṇapratipaddaśāyāṃ praviṣṭaḥ| yasmāt nandābhadrājayāriktāpūrṇātithikrameṇa saṃvṛttibodhicittamṛgāṅkaṃ śoṣaṃ nayatīti| ayamatyarthaṃ kṛṣṇācāryyapādairabhihitaḥ
varagiri-kandara-guhira jagu saela citta ṭṭai|
vimala-salila śoṣa yāiya kālagni paiṭai|
tathāca rativajre—
patite bodhicitte tu sarvvasiddhinidhānake|
mūrcchite skandhavijñāne kutaḥ si[2ka]ddhiraninditā||
tathāca sampuṭodbhavatantrarāje—
analpasaṃkalpatamobhibhūtaṃ
prabhañjanonmattataḍiccalañca|
rāgādidurvvāramalāvaliptaṃ
cittaṃ hi saṃsāramuvāca vajrī||
tasmāt ye kecit prādeśikāḥ paripakvakuśalāḥ bhagavataḥ pañcakramapraveśopāyadhāraṇapūrvveṇa yuganaddharūpaṃ sahajānandaphalaṃ satatamanveṣayanti te'pi vajropa[ma]samādhiṃ sākṣāt kurvvanti| āryyadevapādairapyuktaṃ pañcakramānupūrvveṇa vinā niṣpannakramasambodhi[ṃ] sākṣātkarttuṃ na prāpyate|
segments.translation:
[Rāga]{raga} [Paṭamañjarī]{patamanjari}. 'The body is a [fine tree]{taruvara}', and so on. His heart soothed and sated by the flood of nectar drops from the lotus feet of his glorious [guru]{guru}, and stilled in [joy]{ananda}, and longing to rescue the helpless and wretched people sunk in the middle of the ocean of confusion and great delusion about the [two truths]{satyadvaya}, the [siddha]{siddha} master, the venerable [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, says 'The body', and so on, in order to lead them in as his vow impelled him, and to compose in the vernacular, under the guise of a body-tree, an introduction to the pure nature of reality. The five [aggregates]{skandha}, beginning with form. The six senses, the elements and the sense objects are taken as the [fine tree]{taruvara} of the body, because its leaves are marked by [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka} and by grasping. But a tree is insentient: how can the body be a [fine tree]{taruvara}? That is no fault.
For in just this way even the authors of outside treatises, devoted to the figure of speech called utprekṣā, have declared that likeness rests on some difference. All the more so in its case, for through restlessness, under the sway of the fault of the natural appearances, [Rāhu]{p-rahu} takes, for an ordinary being, the form of falling. He is [Death]{kala}. He enters at the first lunar day of the dark fortnight, for through the sequence of the lunar days Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā and Pūrṇā he brings the [moon]{moon} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} to drying up. The venerable master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has spoken of him forcefully:
In the deep cave of the great mountain the whole world, the [mind]{citta}, breaks;
the pure water dries up when the fire of time enters.
And so in the [Rativajra]{tx-rativajra}:
When [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, the treasury of all [accomplishments]{siddhi}, has fallen
and the consciousness of the [aggregates]{skandha} has swooned, where can blameless [accomplishment]{siddhi} come from?
And so in the king of tantras, the [Sampuṭodbhava]{tx-samputa}:
Overcome by the darkness of countless concepts,
restless as lightning driven wild by the storm wind,
smeared with the stubborn stains of passion and the rest:
this [mind]{citta}, said the holder of the [vajra]{vajra}, is [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
Therefore, whoever among those of limited scope have ripened roots of virtue and, first taking up the means of entering the [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat}'s [five stages]{pancakrama}, constantly seek the fruit, [innate joy]{sahajananda}, whose form is [coupled union]{yuganaddha}: they too directly realize the [vajra]{vajra}-like [samādhi]{samadhi}. The venerable [Āryadeva]{p-aryadeva} too has said: 'Without the [five stages]{pancakrama} in their order, one cannot come to realize directly the awakening of the [completion stage]{nispannakrama}.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads the five branches as the five [aggregates]{skandha} and the body-tree as senses, elements and objects, its leaves being grasped, grasper and grasping: a poetic figure. [Death]{kala} entering the restless [mind]{citta} is [Rāhu]{p-rahu}, who from the dark fortnight's first day dries up the [moon]{moon} of [conventional]{samvrti} [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}. [Innate joy]{sahajananda} is reached through the [five stages]{pancakrama}.

equations.en: the five aggregates, beginning with form
the six senses, the elements and the sense objects, taken as the fine tree of the body, its leaves marked by the grasped, the grasper and grasping
Rāhu, who enters on the first lunar day of the dark fortnight
conventional bodhicitta, pictured as the moon that Rāhu dries up

citations.quoted: varagiri-kandara-guhira jagu saela citta ṭṭai … (In the deep cave of the great mountain …)
citations.work: Kṛṣṇācārya (Kāṇha), an Apabhraṃśa verse; perhaps from his Dohākoṣa

citations.quoted: patite bodhicitte tu sarvvasiddhinidhānake … (When bodhicitta … has fallen …)
citations.work: Rativajra (so named by Munidatta; the work is not otherwise identified)

citations.quoted: analpasaṃkalpatamobhibhūtaṃ … (Overcome by the darkness of countless concepts …)
citations.work: Sampuṭodbhava, 'king of tantras' (probably the Saṃpuṭa Tantra)

citations.quoted: pañcakramānupūrvveṇa vinā niṣpannakramasambodhiṃ … (Without the five stages in their order …)
citations.work: Āryadeva (work not named; perhaps the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa)

flags.note: kimutāsya … prākṛtasattvenācyutirūpo hi rāhuḥ: as printed, acyuti- means 'not falling, imperishable', which makes little sense here unless it alludes to Rāhu's immortality in myth. I read cyuti- 'falling' (the loss of bodhicitta), which fits the drying of the moon and the Rativajra verse on fallen bodhicitta that follows, and take the instrumental prākṛtasattvena as 'for an ordinary being'. The whole sentence is syntactically loose and may be corrupt.

prakṛtyābhāṣa: the scribe interchanges s and ṣ (compare prākṛtabhāsayā for -bhāṣayā, suddha for śuddha), so this is probably prakṛtyābhāsa, the tantric pair of 'natural states' (prakṛti) and 'appearances' (ābhāsa). Rendered 'natural appearances'; a more technical rendering may be wanted.

Kāṇha's Apabhraṃśa couplet, first line: 'citta ṭṭai' looks damaged (perhaps cittu tuṭṭai, 'the mind breaks'), and how jagu saela 'the whole world' relates to citta is unclear. I translate tentatively, keeping world and mind in apposition. In the second line yāiya is taken as jāi jaï, 'goes (dry), when'.

suddhadharmmatāpīṭhikāṃ: pīṭhikā can mean 'introduction, preface' (chosen, since this is the first song) or 'seat, pedestal' ('a seat for the pure nature of reality'), which would anticipate the seat of the last couplet.
praṇidhipreritāvatāraṇārthaṃ: taken as 'to lead them in (to the teaching), as his vow impelled him'. It could also mean 'for the sake of a descent (into the world) prompted by his vow'.

gṛhītaḥ is masculine singular although its subjects (senses, elements, objects) are plural; the body (kāyaḥ) seems to be understood. In nanvacetanatvāt the subject of 'insentient' is unexpressed; I take it as the tree.
prādeśikāḥ: 'of limited scope or capacity' (chosen, given te'pi 'they too'); it could also mean practitioners of a partial path, or simply 'of a certain region'.

Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā and Pūrṇā are the names of the five classes of lunar days, repeated three times through a fortnight; kept as names. ayam (masculine) in ayamatyarthaṃ … abhihitaḥ is taken as referring to Rāhu/Kāla, the subject of Kāṇha's verse.

segments.translit:
diṭakarītyādi| anenopāśakasaṃvarādyanupūrvvā yathā paripāṭyābhiṣikto yogivaraḥ samayasaṅketadravyāpahāreṇa sadgurumārādhyārddharātrau prajñājñānābhiṣeka[ṃ] labdhvā dṛḍhaṃ yathā bhavati| tathā mahāsukhaṃ caturthānanda[ṃ] tvaṃ parimāṇaya|
bhaṇai lui ityādi| tasmin kuliśāravindasaṃyogākṣarasukhopāyaṃ (sukhoya) śrīgurūn pṛṣṭvā viramānande vyāpyavyāpakatayā sarvvadharmmā[3]nupalambharūpaṃ sahajānandamahāsukhaṃ aharniśaṃ jānīhi|
tathāca śrīsamāje—
na vinā vajraguruṇā sarvvakleśaprahāṇakaṃ|
nirvvāṇañca padaṃ śāntamavaivarttikamāpnuyāt||
tathāca nāgārjjunapādaiḥ vajrajāpe coktaṃ—
girīndramūrddhnaḥ prapatettu kaścit
neccheccyutiṃ hi cyavate tathāpi|
guruprasādāptahitopadeśaḥ
icchenna mokṣañca tathāpi muktaḥ||
sarahapādairapyuktaṃ prabandhe—
yā sā saṃsāracakraṃ viracayati manaḥsanniyogātmahetoḥ
sā dhīryasya[āḥ] prasādāddiśati nijabhuvaṃ svāmino niṣprapañca[ṃ]|
tacca pratyātmavedyaṃ samudayati sukhaṃ kalpanājā(ma)lamuktaṃ
kuryyāt tasyāṃhriyugmaṃ śirasi savinayaṃ sadguroḥ sarvvakālaṃ||
śrīhevajre'pi—
ātmanā jñāyate puṇyāt guruparvvopasevayā|
segments.translation:
'Make it firm', and so on. This means: you, an excellent yogin who has received [empowerment]{abhiseka} step by step in due order, in the sequence that begins with the lay vows, having pleased the true [guru]{guru} with an offering of the [pledge]{samaya} substances agreed by sign, and having received the wisdom-knowledge [empowerment]{abhiseka} at midnight, should take the measure of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the fourth [joy]{ananda}, in such a way that it becomes firm.
'[Lūyī]{p-luyi} says', and so on. In that state, having asked the glorious [guru]{guru} about the means to the imperishable bliss of the union of [vajra]{vajra} and lotus, know day and night, in the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, the [great bliss]{mahasukha} of [innate joy]{sahajananda}, whose form, by way of pervaded and pervader, is the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
And so in the glorious [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}:
Without the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru} one cannot reach
[nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, the peaceful state from which there is no turning back, which removes all [afflictions]{klesa}.
And so the venerable [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} has said on [vajra]{vajra} recitation:
Should someone fall from the summit of the king of mountains,
though he does not wish to fall, he falls all the same;
one who has gained helpful [instruction]{upadesa} by the [guru]{guru}'s grace,
though he does not wish for liberation, is liberated all the same.
The venerable [Saraha]{p-saraha} too has said in a composition:
The intellect that, yoked to the mind as its cause, fashions the wheel of [saṃsāra]{samsara},
that same intellect, by his grace, points to the lord's own ground, free of elaboration,
and brings forth a bliss to be known by each within, freed from the net of concepts:
at all times, with humility, one should place on one's head the two feet of that true [guru]{guru}.
In the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra} too:
It is known by oneself, through merit, by attending on the [guru]{guru} at the proper times.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as addressed to the yogin who, having received the wisdom-knowledge [empowerment]{abhiseka} at midnight, must take the measure of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, the fourth [joy]{ananda}, and make it firm. Asking the [guru]{guru} is learning the way to the bliss of [vajra]{vajra}-and-lotus union, and then knowing [innate joy]{sahajananda} day and night. His quotations make the guru indispensable.

citations.quoted: na vinā vajraguruṇā sarvvakleśaprahāṇakaṃ … (Without the vajra guru …)
girīndramūrddhnaḥ prapatettu kaścit … (Should someone fall from the summit of the king of mountains …)
citations.work: Nāgārjuna, on vajra recitation (vajrajāpa); probably the Vajrajāpakrama, first chapter of the Pañcakrama

citations.quoted: yā sā saṃsāracakraṃ viracayati … (The intellect that fashions the wheel of saṃsāra …)
citations.work: Saraha, an unnamed composition (prabandha); a Sanskrit verse in sragdharā metre, not one of the Apabhraṃśa dohās

citations.quoted: ātmanā jñāyate puṇyāt guruparvvopasevayā (It is known by oneself, through merit …)

flags.note: samayasaṅketadravyāpahāreṇa: apahāra 'removal, theft' gives no sense; I read upahāra 'offering' (dravyopahāreṇa).

The first sentence has a nominative yogivaraḥ with absolutives but ends in a second-person imperative (tvaṃ parimāṇaya); I take the yogin as the one addressed. dṛḍhaṃ yathā bhavati ('so that it becomes firm') glosses diṭa and may attach either to the empowerment or to the measuring of great bliss; I attach it to the latter, as the song does.

'(sukhoya)' after kuliśāravindasaṃyogākṣarasukhopāyaṃ is a parenthesis in Shastri, probably recording the manuscript's reading or an alternative (perhaps akṣarasukho 'yaṃ, 'this is imperishable bliss'). I translate the main text, sukhopāyaṃ, 'the means to the bliss'.
śrīgurūn is plural, surely honorific; rendered 'the glorious guru'. tasmin is rendered 'in that state'; its referent (the fourth joy?) is not stated.
Saraha's verse, line 2: Shastri restores yasya[āḥ] (feminine), but the correlative tasya … sadguroḥ in line 4 requires masculine yasya, 'by whose (the guru's) grace'. I translate yasya.
Saraha's verse, line 3: kalpanājā(ma)la. The sragdharā metre requires kalpanājāla 'net of concepts'; kalpanāmala 'stain of concepts' does not scan. I translate jāla.
manaḥsanniyogātmahetoḥ is obscure: 'yoked to the mind as its cause' (chosen); alternatively 'by reason of the joining of mind and self', or 'for its own sake, through joining with the mind'.

Hevajra half-verse: guruparvvopasevayā, 'attending on the guru at the proper times (parvan)', translated as printed; it could be a slip for gurupādopasevayā, 'serving at the guru's feet'. Only this half-verse is quoted and its subject is not stated, so the segment may end abruptly in the manuscript.

segments.translit:
padāntareṇa mahārāganayasamādhyuddīpayannanuśaṃsāmāha|
saala samāhītyādi| bhagavataiva nayabhedenānaṃtāparyyantāḥ samādhayo daśākuśalaparihārāya indriyanirodhāya nirddiṣṭāḥ| tai[3ka]ratra samādhibhiḥ mahārāganaye sukharahitatvāt duṣkarapoṣadhādiniyamaiśca kiñcinna kriyate||
ataḥ śrīsamāje—
duṣkarairnniyamaistīvrairmūrttiḥ śuṣyati duḥkhitā|
duḥkhāddhi kṣipyate cittaṃ vikṣepāt siddhiranyathā|| iti|
tathāca śrīhevajre—
rāgeṇa badhyate loko rāgeṇaiva vimucyate|
viparītabhāvanā hyeṣā na jñātā buddhatīrthikaiḥ||
iti| evaṃ mahāsukhāvaghātena rahitatvena buddhatīrthiko bahūni duḥkhānyanubhūya utpadyante mriyante ca| na te tasya bhāginaḥ|
tathācāgamaḥ—
tattvahīnā na siddhyanti kalpakoṭiśatairapītivacanāt| mahārā[ga]nayacaryyāmapyāha—
śrīsamāje—
pañca kāmān parityajya tapobhirna ca pīḍayet|
sukhena sādhayed bodhiṃ yogatantrānusārataḥ||
tathāca sarahapādaiḥ—
tanutaracittāṅkurako viṣayarasairyadi na sicyate śuddhaiḥ|
gaganavyāpī phaladaḥ kalpatarutvaṃ kathaṃ labhate||
segments.translation:
With the next [verse]{pada}, bringing to light the [samādhi]{samadhi} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}, he states its benefit.
'All the [samādhis]{samadhi}', and so on. The [Blessed One]{p-bhagavat} himself, according to the differences between approaches, taught endless, boundless [samādhis]{samadhi} for avoiding the ten non-virtues and for restraining the senses. Here, on the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}, nothing at all is achieved by those [samādhis]{samadhi}, since they lack bliss, nor by the arduous poṣadha fast and other such observances.
Hence in the glorious [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}:
Through harsh and arduous observances the body suffers and withers;
suffering distracts the [mind]{citta}, and through distraction [accomplishment]{siddhi} goes astray.
And so in the glorious [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
By passion the world is bound; by passion itself it is freed.
This reversed meditation is not known to Buddhists and [tīrthikas]{tirthika}.
Thus, deprived of [great bliss]{mahasukha} by its obstruction, Buddhists and [tīrthikas]{tirthika} experience many sufferings, and are born and die. They have no share in it.
And so scripture, for it is said: 'Those who lack the truth do not succeed, even in billions of aeons.' He also teaches the [conduct]{carya} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}, in the glorious [Guhyasamāja]{tx-guhyasamaja}:
One should not give up the five sense pleasures and torment oneself with austerities;
one should accomplish awakening through bliss, following the yoga tantras.
And so the venerable [Saraha]{p-saraha}:
If the tender sprout of the [mind]{citta} is not watered with the pure juices of the sense objects,
how will it become a wish-granting tree that fills the sky and bears fruit?
segments.note: Munidatta reads the couplet as praising the [samādhi]{samadhi} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}. The countless samādhis taught for avoiding non-virtue and restraining the senses, like harsh fasts, achieve nothing here, since they lack bliss; without [great bliss]{mahasukha}, Buddhists and [tīrthikas]{tirthika} suffer, are born and die. Passion itself frees, and awakening is won through bliss.

equations.en: the endless samādhis the Blessed One taught for avoiding the ten non-virtues and restraining the senses

citations.quoted: duṣkarairnniyamaistīvrairmūrttiḥ śuṣyati duḥkhitā … (Through harsh and arduous observances …)
rāgeṇa badhyate loko rāgeṇaiva vimucyate … (By passion the world is bound …)
tattvahīnā na siddhyanti kalpakoṭiśatairapi (Those who lack the truth do not succeed …)
pañca kāmān parityajya tapobhirna ca pīḍayet … (One should not give up the five sense pleasures …)
tanutaracittāṅkurako viṣayarasairyadi na sicyate śuddhaiḥ … (If the tender sprout of the mind …)
citations.work: Saraha; probably a Sanskrit rendering of one of his dohās

flags.note: mahāsukhāvaghātena rahitatvena: avaghāta 'striking down, obstruction' is awkward. It may be an error for mahāsukhāvagāhena, 'because they lack immersion in great bliss'. I translate the printed text ('deprived of great bliss by its obstruction').

buddhatīrthiko is singular but its verbs (utpadyante, mriyante) and the following te are plural; I take it, as in the Hevajra verse, as 'Buddhists and tīrthikas'. 'Buddhist tīrthikas' (heterodox Buddhists) is also possible.

pañca kāmān parityajya tapobhirna ca pīḍayet: I take the negative as governing both the absolutive and the verb ('one should not give up the five sense pleasures and torment oneself'). Read positively ('having given up the five sense pleasures') it would contradict the next line and Munidatta's point.
mahārāganayasamādhyuddīpayan: samādhim would be expected; the compound is irregular but the sense is clear. anuśaṃsā is taken in its Buddhist sense 'benefit, advantage' rather than 'praise'.

segments.translit:
mahārāganayacaryyārthaniṣyandisākṣātpramāṇānyanyeṣāṃ vita[4]thajñānābhiniviṣṭānāṃ āgrahakhaṇḍanārthaṃ tṛtīyapadamāha|
eṛieu ityādi| paścācchandamoḍḍiyānakaraṇādibandhaṃvihāya śūnyatāpakṣaketi nairātmadharmma pāśamiti samīpaṃ tadīyāliṅganaṃ kuru| re saṃbodhanaṃ| bho mokṣaśīlāḥ|
tathācāgamaḥ—
etāni tāni śikharāṇi samunnatāni
satkāyadṛṣṭivipulācalasaṃsthitāni|
nairātmabodhakuliśena vidāritātmā
bhedamprayāti sahajairapi duḥkhaśailaiḥ||
segments.translation:
To break the stubbornness of others, who cling to false knowledge, he speaks the third [verse]{pada}: direct proofs that flow from the meaning of the [conduct]{carya} of the [way of great passion]{maharaganaya}.
'Let go', and so on. Then, giving up desire and the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna: 'the side of [emptiness]{sunyata}' means the teaching of [selflessness]{nairatmya}; 'pāsa' means near: embrace it. 'Re' is a form of address: 'O you who are intent on liberation!'
And so scripture:
These are those towering peaks
that stand on the vast mountain of the view of a real self.
Its body split by the [vajra]{vajra} of realizing [selflessness]{nairatmya},
it breaks apart, together with the mountains of suffering born with it.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the couplet as breaking the obstinacy of those who cling to false knowledge. One must give up desire and the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna; 'the side of [emptiness]{sunyata}' is the teaching of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, to be embraced; 're' addresses those intent on liberation. A quoted verse has selflessness shatter the view of a real self.

equations.en: desire, and the bonds of practices such as oḍḍiyāna
a vocative: 'O you who are intent on liberation'

citations.quoted: etāni tāni śikharāṇi samunnatāni … (These are those towering peaks …)

flags.note: Printed nairātmadharmmapāśamiti is divided as nairātmadharma | pāśam iti samīpaṃ: 'the side of emptiness means the teaching of selflessness; pāsa (the song's word, with ś for s) means near'. Taking it as one compound, 'the noose of the dharma of selflessness', gives poor sense and leaves the song's pāsa unglossed. My translit shows the division.

oḍḍiyānakaraṇādibandhaṃ: oḍḍiyāna is probably the yogic 'lock' (uḍḍiyāna-bandha), counted among bodily techniques (karaṇa); Oḍḍiyāna the sacred site is possible but fits bandha less well. Kept in source form. paścāt 'then' glosses no word of the song, and pāṭera āsa is not glossed at all.

nairātmadharma is marked as selflessness (nairatmya), the doctrine. The command to embrace it may evoke the goddess Nairātmā (nairatma), but the segment does not name her. dharma is rendered 'teaching'; 'reality' or 'nature' is possible.

sahajairapi in the verse is the ordinary adjective 'born with (it)', describing the mountains of suffering, not the technical 'innate' of the glossary entry sahaja; I left it unmarked to avoid a misleading link.
sākṣātpramāṇāni (neuter plural) stands loosely beside tṛtīyapadam as a second object of āha; taken as in apposition, 'the third verse: direct proofs …'.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena yathābhūtadharmmyamāhātmyadṛṣṭapratyayatāmāha—
bhaṇai ityādi|—ādisiddhācāryyalūyīpāda evaṃ vadati, mayā lūyīpādena siddhācāryyeṇa dhyānavaseneti| manovijñāne viṣayendriyavalayatvāt| śrīgurau caturthopadeśalabdhābhyāsena yuganaddharūpaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ|
tathā cāgame—
indriyāṇi svapantīva manontarviśatīva ca|
naṣṭaceṣṭa ivābhāti kāyaḥ satsukhamūrcchitaḥ||
dhavanaṃ śaśiśuddhyālinā cavaṇaṃ raviśu[4ka]ddhyā kālinā tadubhābhyāmāsanaṃ kṛtvā svadevatāhaṅkāropaviṣṭaḥ san sākṣāt kṛtaṃ|
tathāca dvikalpe—
ālikālisamāyogo vajrasattvasya viṣṭaraṃ iti||1||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of the conviction that comes from having seen the greatness of reality as it truly is.
'Says', and so on. The first [siddha]{siddha} master, the venerable [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, says this: 'by me, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Lūyī]{p-luyi}, through the power of meditation'; for in mental consciousness the sense objects and the senses are dissolved. Through practising the fourth [instruction]{upadesa}, received from the glorious [guru]{guru}, the form of [coupled union]{yuganaddha} was seen.
And so in scripture:
The senses seem to sleep, and the mind seems to enter within;
the body, swooning in true bliss, looks as if all its movement were gone.
The [dhamaṇa]{dhamana} is [āli]{ali}, through the purification of the [moon]{moon}; the [camaṇa]{camana} is [kāli]{kali}, through the purification of the [sun]{surya}. Making a seat of the two, and seated in the pride of being his own deity, he realized it directly.
And so in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}:
The union of [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali} is the seat of [Vajrasattva]{p-vajrasattva}.
segments.note: Munidatta hears [Lūyī]{p-luyi} testify to what he saw through the power of meditation: [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, reached by practising the fourth [instruction]{upadesa} received from the [guru]{guru}. He reads [dhamaṇa]{dhamana} and [camaṇa]{camana} as [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali}, with the purification of the moon and the sun; seated on these two in the pride of his own deity, Lūyī realized it directly.

equations.en: the form of coupled union, seen through practising the fourth instruction received from the guru
āli, through the purification of the moon
kāli, through the purification of the sun
a seat (āsana) made of the two

citations.quoted: indriyāṇi svapantīva manontarviśatīva ca … (The senses seem to sleep …)
ālikālisamāyogo vajrasattvasya viṣṭaraṃ (The union of āli and kāli is the seat of Vajrasattva)

flags.note: manovijñāne viṣayendriyavalayatvāt: valaya 'ring, enclosure' gives little sense; I read vilaya 'dissolution' ('because objects and senses are dissolved in mental consciousness'), which the verse that follows (the senses asleep, the mind gone within) supports.

Munidatta writes dhavana and cavaṇa for the song's dhamaṇa and camaṇa; I used the glossary forms dhamaṇa and camaṇa in the translation. The instrumentals śaśiśuddhyālinā / raviśuddhyā kālinā could also be construed 'the seat is made of dhavana by means of āli …'; the identification is the same either way.
sākṣāt kṛtaṃ is an impersonal passive with no expressed object; I supply 'he' and 'it' (coupled union, from the preceding sentence). śrīgurau (locative) is rendered 'received from the glorious guru'.
yathābhūtadharmmyamāhātmyadṛṣṭapratyayatām: rendered 'the conviction that comes from having seen the greatness of reality as it truly is'; dharmmya may be an error for dharma or dharmatā.
The closing ||1|| marks the end of the commentary on song 1 and is not translated.

proposals.definition: Munidatta's word for a couplet of a song, used when he turns to comment on it ('with the next verse', 'the third verse'). In song 1 he calls couplets 4 and 5 the third and fourth, so he counts the opening couplet as the first and leaves the refrain out of the count.
proposals.rationale: The word introduces Munidatta's comment on most couplets in every song, so a fixed rendering keeps his structural cues consistent. Match only these compounds: pada also means 'state' (nirvāṇa padaṃ, cp.01.m3), which should not link here.

proposals.definition: Instruction: the practical, often oral, teaching a guru gives a disciple for yogic practice. Munidatta quotes Nāgārjuna on helpful instruction gained by the guru's grace (cp.01.m3), and says Lūyī saw coupled union by practising the fourth instruction received from the guru (cp.01.m6).
proposals.rationale: Recurs in the commentary (the keruala entry already speaks of the instruction of the Five Stages at cp.14.m4); a fixed rendering keeps it distinct from general words for teaching.

proposals.definition: The commitments a tantric initiate takes on, and by extension the ritual substances bound up with them. Munidatta says the yogin pleases the true guru with an offering of pledge substances before receiving the wisdom-knowledge empowerment (cp.01.m3).
proposals.rationale: A standard tantric term likely to recur; the abhiseka entry already speaks of 'pledge substances'. Match narrowly, since samaya also means 'time'.

proposals.definition: The completion stage: the phase of tantric yoga that follows the visualization of the deity and works with the subtle body toward realization. Munidatta cites Āryadeva: its awakening cannot be realized without passing through the five stages in order (cp.01.m2).
proposals.rationale: Technical term likely to recur beside the five stages (pancakrama); a fixed English keeps the two apart.

questions: Name forms: to follow the glossary rule I rendered Munidatta's Kṛṣṇācārya as Kāṇha, Śrī Samāja as Guhyasamāja, Dvikalpa as Hevajra, and his spellings dhavana and cavaṇa as dhamaṇa and camaṇa. Should the commentary keep his own forms, with them added to the glossary as variants?

kāla: 'Death' hides Munidatta's link between Kāla (whom he identifies with Rāhu) and the kālāgni, 'fire of time', of Kāṇha's verse (cp.01.m2). Would 'Time', or keeping 'Kāla', serve better here? I left 'fire of time' unlinked because it is not the approved English.

Pada count: Munidatta calls couplet 4 the third verse and couplet 5 the fourth, so he counts couplet 1 as the first and skips the refrain. The text brief says he counts from the couplet after the refrain. Please confirm which is right, and whether 'verse' (proposed id pada) is acceptable.

Line 4a: Munidatta takes karaṇa as bodily techniques such as oḍḍiyāna (probably the yogic 'lock') and gives chanda 'desire' for chāndaka; he does not gloss pāṭera āsa. This may bear on the draft's 'hope in the rules of practice'.

lotus: I left 'lotus' unlinked in 'lotus feet' and 'lotus mouth' (m1, m2) and in 'the union of vajra and lotus' (m3), because the lotus entry describes the flower of song 10. Should the vajra-lotus union link to it, or have its own entry?

First-gloss terms (siddha, vajra, rāga, samādhi, bodhicitta, āli, kāli, dhamaṇa, camaṇa): the weave schema has no field for a first-occurrence gloss, so I relied on the glossary links. Is a gloss wanted inside the woven notes?

Emendations: I translated emended readings where the printed text gave no sense (acyuti to cyuti in m2, apahāra to upahāra in m3, yasyāḥ to yasya in m3, valaya to vilaya in m6) but kept the printed avaghāta in m4. Please confirm whether the commentary should follow emendations or the printed text, with the alternative in a note.
